full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: This appeal by the accused-appellants following leave raises the question as to whether following stoppage of proceedings and release of the accused under section 339C(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, shortly, the Code, a fresh complaint/proceeding against the same set of accused persons by the same set of complainants upon the self-same allegations is permissible or not. It arises from the judgment and order dated 2l.7.86 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka Bench in Criminal Revision No. 29 of 1986 discharging the Rule obtained under sections 435/439 of the Code and refusing to interfere with the order dated 12.1.86 framing charge against the appellants in Petition Case No. 721a of 1985 under sections 448/227 of the Penal Code by Mr. MA Matin Chowdhury, Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. 

 2. Earlier, respondent No. 1 lodged an FIR against the accused-appellants alleging trespass, etc. giving rise to Motijheel PS Case No. 2 (4)85. After investigation the police submitted charge-sheet against the accused-appellants under sections 147/ 447/427/448/241/380 of the Penal Code. The case was pending before the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. By order dated 19-8-85, further proceeding in respect of the trial was stopped and the accused-appellants were released by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate under section 339C(4) of the Code. Respondent No. 1 thereafter filed a fresh petition of complaint before the same Court against the appellants on the self-same allegations. The Metropolitan Magistrate after examining the respondent ob solemn affirmation on 9-9-85, called for the previous records and summons were issued. By the impugned order dated 12-1-86 charge was framed against the accused-appellants under sections 448/427 of the Penal Code by Mr. MA Matin Chowdhury, Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. The resultant Rule in Criminal Revision No. 29 of 1986 was discharged by the learned Single Judge on the ground that the accused-appellants having been neither acquitted nor convicted, section 403 of the Code is not applicable and filing of a fresh complaint on the self-same allegations is not barred by law. 

 7. When a proceeding is stopped either under section 249 or 339C of the Code, without pronouncing any judgment either of acquittal or of conviction and the accused is released, it does not operate either as a discharge or as an acquittal of the accused, so as to attract in the latter case the protection of section 403 of the Code barring trial for the same offence once convicted or acquitted. Stoppage of a proceeding and release of the accused stand short of a discharge. It is a half-way to discharge, but not discharge proper. It is certainly not an acquittal. The proceeding is not brought to a close. It does not fade into a past and closed transaction. The same proceeding, however, cannot be revived unless there is a legislative mandate to that effect. By Ordinance No. XXIII of 1986, dated 27.3.86, section 339D was inserted in the Code providing for revival within 90 days of those proceedings in respect of which trial was stopped. Section 339D, however, has no application in the present case because the earlier proceeding was stopped on 19.8.85 and Ordinance No. XXIII of 1986 came into operation on 27.3.86. A proceeding can be revived under Ordinance No. XXIII of 1986 within 90 days of the date of stoppage, but in the present case, more than 90 days had already elapsed before Ordinance No. XXIII of 1986 came into force. The revival of the same proceeding being out of question in the present case, there was no bar in law against institution of a fresh complaint on the same allegations. Mr. Nabi's submission that the Code does not in terms permit the complainant to institute a fresh proceeding is not the correct way to look at the legislation. In view of the fact that the accused- appellants were neither acquitted nor convicted, the correct way of looking at the legislation is to see whether the legislature created a fresh bar, in the nature of section 403 or analogous to it, prohibiting a fresh proceeding. The legislature created no such bar and that is the yardstick with which the intention of the legislature is to be read. Mr. Nabi's submission that the manifest intention of the legislature in enacting Section 339C was to put an end to the harassment of an accused of fresh trial on the same allegations beyond the stipulated period is not at all borne out by the use of the words 'further proceedings in respect of the trial shall stand stopped and the accused persons released'. These words in fact mean that the proceeding in question has come to a stop and the same proceeding can only be revived if the legislature gives its sanctions to it, but the words quoted do not mean that fresh proceeding cannot be started on the same allegations. A fresh proceeding' and 'further proceedings in respect of the trial' do not mean the same thing. Mr. Nabi, however, made desperate efforts to distinguish between the provisions of sections 249 and 339C of the Code, but the legal effect of the above-quoted words in section 339C and the provisions of section 249 remains the same, namely, that the same proceeding can be revived by a legislative mandate or, in the alternative, a fresh proceeding can be instituted on the same allegations. It appears to us that section 339C was enacted in order to inject a spirit of utmost expedition, speed and urgency in the trial of criminal cases, but it does not appear from the language used in section 339C that it was the intention of the legislature to bid a fare well to the well-known concept of criminal jurisprudence that a criminal complaint suffers from no law of limitation and that an alleged criminal act will never go untried. The manifest intention of the legislature is further evidenced by the enactment of Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1983 on 8.8.83 whereby it was provided that the trial of any case pending on 8.8.83 before a Sessions Judge, etc. shall continue and be concluded before, 31.12.83. By further amending Ordinances this date was periodically extended. Finally by enacting Ordinance No. XXIII of 1986 on 22.3.86 the legislature inserted section 339D of the Code to provide for revival of cases stopped under section 339C(4) within 90 days from the date of stoppage. These legislative exercises, therefore, are meant to energise and activate the criminal Courts in the disposal of cases and are not meant to give any false hope to the accused that the arms of law will not reach them at all once the stipulated period is over. 

 8. Mr. Nabi, however, relies upon case of Md. Zoha @ Shamsuzzoha and another Vs. The State, 33 DLR 205, a decision of a Division Bench of the High Court Division, Rangpur Bench, in support of his submission that instead of filing a fresh proceeding the complainant-respondent No.1 could have prayed for revival of the previous proceeding. The argument is misconceived. The above-cited case was decided on the footing that the case which was stopped was a pending case when Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1983 came into effect on 8.8.83 and, therefore, the Government rightly moved the Sessions Judge on 9.11.83 for revival of the stopped case. The accused-appellants cannot get the benefit of Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1983 because this was simply not a case which was pending on 8.8.83. 

 9. In view of the discussion above, the question raised in this appeal is answered in the affirmative and we hold that there is no legal bar for instituting a fresh prosecution on the self-same facts after a proceeding is stopped and accused released under section 339C (4) of the Code. But whether cognizance should or should not be taken in such a case, of necessity, must depend on the facts and circumstances of each particular case and the provision as to revival of proceeding as amended, compliance or non-compliance therewith and other related considerations will all be brought to bear at the time of taking cognizance a second time against the accused. It may be observed that generally a fresh cognizance should not be taken where a proceeding for revival could be taken but was not taken without sufficient cause or where the revived proceeding terminates again in stoppage of the same. We, therefore, find no ground for interference with the judgment and order of the High Court Division.
